antiExamples.name: Setting size on an individual avatar item
antiExamples.reason: AvatarGroupItem omits size from Avatar's own props - Avatar Group applies one size uniformly via AvatarGroupProps.size, including to the overflow trigger. There is no per-avatar size mixing, matching Figma's own avatar-group example.

antiExamples.name: Expecting a truncated avatar's selection to navigate automatically
antiExamples.reason: Selecting a truncated avatar from the overflow panel only calls onOverflowAvatarSelect(avatar, event) - Avatar Group does not read the avatar's own data and navigate for you, the same 'never assume' rule Menu's own onSelect follows.

examples.name: An active filter
examples.description: The common case - a property name plus its current value, editable in place via the value segment's own menu.
examples.jsx:
<Chip
  mode="filter"
  label="Status"
  elemBefore={<TaskNotStartedIcon decorative />}
  value={{
    label: '2 statuses',
    sections: [
      {
        id: 'statuses',
        items: [
          { id: 'not-started', label: 'Not started', onSelect: () => toggleStatus('not-started') },
          { id: 'in-progress', label: 'In progress', onSelect: () => toggleStatus('in-progress') },
        ],
      },
    ],
  }}
  onRemove={() => clearFilter('status')}
/>

examples.name: A filter with a comparison operator
examples.description: An optional operator segment sits between the label and the value. Figma only shows this on its due date filter, but nothing about it is date-specific.
examples.jsx:
<Chip
  mode="filter"
  label="Due date"
  elemBefore={<CalendarIcon decorative />}
  operator={{
    label: 'before',
    sections: [{ id: 'ops', items: [{ id: 'on', label: 'on' }, { id: 'before', label: 'before' }, { id: 'after', label: 'after' }] }],
  }}
  value={{ label: 'April 15', sections: dateSections }}
  onRemove={() => clearFilter('due')}
/>

examples.name: A filter whose value has a preview
examples.description: valuePreview renders before the value text - an Avatar, an Avatar Group, status icons. Decorative only; the value text carries the meaning.
examples.jsx:
<Chip
  mode="filter"
  label="Assignee"
  value={{ label: '3 people', sections: peopleSections }}
  valuePreview={
    <AvatarGroup
      size="xs"
      maxVisible={3}
      avatars={[
        { id: 'a', name: 'Jordan Ellis' },
        { id: 'b', name: 'Priya Nair' },
        { id: 'c', name: 'Sam Okafor' },
      ]}
    />
  }
  onRemove={() => clearFilter('assignee')}
/>

examples.name: An applied property
examples.description: The value is the label, so there is nothing to open - the only affordance is removing it.

examples.name: A selectable search scope
examples.description: scope is the only selectable mode - a real toggle button carrying aria-pressed. Chip never changes its own selection; wire onSelectedChange.

examples.name: Smaller size for a dense filter bar
examples.description: size applies to every segment together, matching Figma - there is no per-segment size mixing.
examples.jsx:
<Chip
  mode="filter"
  size="sm"
  label="Status"
  value={{ label: 'Any', sections: statusSections }}
  onRemove={() => clearFilter('status')}
/>

examples.name: Naming a panel explicitly
examples.description: Panels default to `${label} value` / `${label} operator`. Override when the composed name would read poorly, or when label is not a plain string.
examples.jsx: Status} value={{ label: '2 statuses', sections: statusSections, menuAriaLabel: 'Choose statuses' }} removeAriaLabel="Clear the status filter" onRemove={() => clearFilter('status')} />

antiExamples.name: Using Chip as a plain label
antiExamples.reason: Only if there is nothing to remove. A non-removable, non-interactive label is Tag's job - Chip always carries an affordance (remove, or selection for scope), and `onRemove` is required for property/filter precisely because every verified Figma variant has one.

antiExamples.name: Passing filter props to a scope chip
antiExamples.jsx: <Chip mode="scope" label="Matters" value={{ label: 'Any', sections: [] }} onRemove={() => {}} />
antiExamples.reason: ChipProps is a discriminated union on `mode` - `value` and `onRemove` are not part of the scope branch, so TypeScript rejects this at compile time rather than silently ignoring them.

antiExamples.name: Putting an interactive control in elemBefore or valuePreview
antiExamples.reason: Both slots are decorative and aria-hidden. In scope mode the segment is itself a <button>, so nesting a focusable element inside it is invalid HTML - the same rule Menu's own leadingElement follows.

antiExamples.name: Expecting a tone prop
antiExamples.reason: chip-base supports five tones in Figma, but all 14 chip variants use tone=default, so no chip-level tone mapping is verified. Deliberately unexposed until a real Figma chip variant uses one; TypeScript rejects it.

examples.name: A scope selector
examples.description: The common case - independent on/off scope chips sharing one size. Chip Group lays them out; the consumer holds which are on.

examples.name: An active filter bar
examples.description: Filter chips share the group's size; removing one is the consumer's job.
examples.jsx:
<ChipGroup size="md" aria-label="Active filters">
  <Chip
    mode="filter"
    label="Status"
    elemBefore={<TaskNotStartedIcon decorative />}
    value={{ label: '2 statuses', sections: statusSections }}
    onRemove={() => dropFilter('status')}
  />
  <Chip
    mode="filter"
    label="Due date"
    elemBefore={<CalendarIcon decorative />}
    operator={{ label: 'before', sections: operatorSections }}
    value={{ label: 'April 15', sections: dateSections }}
    onRemove={() => dropFilter('due')}
  />
</ChipGroup>

examples.name: Packing chips against the trailing edge
examples.description: alignment maps to justify-content - which edge the chips pack against. Note this is not Tag Group's alignment, which places an overflow tag.
examples.jsx:
<ChipGroup alignment="right" size="md">
  <Chip mode="scope" label="Matters" isSelected />
  <Chip mode="scope" label="Documents" />
</ChipGroup>

examples.name: One chip opting out of the group's size
examples.description: An explicit size on an individual Chip wins, because Chip resolves size ?? groupSize ?? 'md'.
examples.jsx:
<ChipGroup size="sm">
  <Chip mode="scope" label="Inherits sm" />
  <Chip mode="scope" label="Explicitly md" size="md" />
</ChipGroup>

examples.name: Size reaching a wrapped chip
examples.description: Size travels by context, so it still reaches a Chip behind a Tooltip, a fragment, or a conditional - which cloning children would not.
examples.jsx:
<ChipGroup size="sm">
  <Tooltip content="Only matters you own">
    <Chip mode="scope" label="My matters" />
  </Tooltip>
  {showArchived ? <Chip mode="scope" label="Archived" /> : null}
</ChipGroup>

examples.name: Mixed modes in one group
examples.description: Any Chip mode can share a row - the group only lays them out and shares a size.
examples.jsx:
<ChipGroup size="md">
  <Chip mode="scope" label="Matters" isSelected />
  <Chip mode="property" label="Trusts" onRemove={detachTrusts} />
  <Chip mode="filter" label="Status" value={{ label: 'Any', sections: statusSections }} onRemove={clearStatus} />
</ChipGroup>

antiExamples.name: Expecting overflow truncation
antiExamples.reason: Chip Group has no truncation - Figma models none, so all chips wrap onto new lines instead of collapsing behind a "+N more" affordance. `maxVisible` does not exist; use Tag Group (with Tags) when you need that behaviour. TypeScript rejects the prop.

antiExamples.name: Expecting the group to manage selection
antiExamples.reason: Chip Group is layout only. Scope chips are independent on/off toggles, so which are selected is the consumer's state - pass isSelected/onSelectedChange to each Chip, exactly as with Toggle Button.

antiExamples.name: Repeating size on every chip inside a sized group
antiExamples.jsx:
<ChipGroup size="sm">
  <Chip mode="scope" label="Matters" size="sm" />
  <Chip mode="scope" label="Documents" size="sm" />
</ChipGroup>
antiExamples.reason: Redundant - the group already shares its size through context. Setting it per-chip is only for deliberately opting one chip out, and repeating it invites the exact bug the group exists to prevent: one chip missed, breaking the line it wraps onto.

antiExamples.name: Adding padding or a background to the group
antiExamples.reason: Chip Group is pure layout - Figma's own container has zero padding and no fill or stroke. Put the surface on a wrapper you own, so the group keeps hugging its chips.

antiExamples.name: Hover-only reveal

<InlineMessage title="Hint" onMouseEnter={showDetail} />

  onPageChange={setPage}
  ariaLabel="Search results pages"
  previousLabel="Previous results"
  nextLabel="Next results"
/>

antiExamples.name: Single page
antiExamples.reason: Pagination adds navigation overhead with nothing to navigate to - omit it when there's only one page.

antiExamples.name: Infinite scroll content
antiExamples.reason: Pagination expects a known, finite totalPages - use a 'load more' affordance for infinite scroll instead.

examples.name: Default subtle skeleton
examples.description: Default appearance, shape, and sizing (fills its container, one text line tall).

examples.name: Default appearance
examples.description: More visible fill, for a full-page loading state.

examples.name: Circle for an avatar
examples.description: A circular placeholder sized to match an Avatar.

examples.name: A paragraph of text lines
examples.description: Multiple Skeletons of varying width, composed to sketch a paragraph.

examples.name: List row with avatar
examples.description: A circular avatar placeholder next to two text-line placeholders.

examples.name: Labelled for screen readers
examples.description: The sole loading indicator on screen, announced via label.

antiExamples.name: Clickable skeleton
antiExamples.reason: Skeleton is non-interactive; it has no interactive behavior and is not meant to receive input.

antiExamples.name: Text content
antiExamples.reason: Skeleton has no children slot - it is the placeholder shape itself, not a text container.

antiExamples.name: Visible loading copy next to a labelled Skeleton
antiExamples.reason: The label prop already announces the loading state to assistive technology - duplicating it as visible text is redundant and should instead rely on adjacent context or the label alone.

examples.name: Primary action with closely related alternatives
examples.description: The common case - a labeled primary action plus a small group of alternatives reachable from the caret segment.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton
  secondaryActionLabel="More save options"
  sections={[
    {
      id: 'save-options',
      items: [
        { id: 'save-as', label: 'Save as...', onSelect: () => saveAs() },
        { id: 'save-copy', label: 'Save a copy', onSelect: () => saveCopy() },
      ],
    },
  ]}
  onClick={() => save()}
>
  Save
</SplitButton>

examples.name: Primary appearance
examples.description: appearance applies uniformly to both segments, matching every verified Figma variant.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton
  appearance="primary"
  secondaryActionLabel="More send options"
  sections={sendAlternatives}
  onClick={() => sendForSignature()}
>
  Send for signature
</SplitButton>

examples.name: Smaller size for a dense toolbar
examples.description: size applies uniformly to both segments, matching Button's own four sizes exactly.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton size="sm" secondaryActionLabel="More options" sections={alternatives} onClick={() => create()}>
  Create
</SplitButton>

examples.name: Loading primary action
examples.description: isLoading applies Button's own loading treatment to the primary action and also disables the secondary action - picking an alternative while the primary action is mid-flight would be confusing.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton isLoading secondaryActionLabel="More save options" sections={saveAlternatives} onClick={() => save()}>
  Saving...
</SplitButton>

examples.name: Disabling both segments together
examples.description: disabled disables both segments together (native disabled on both), matching how Figma's own isDisabled axis covers the whole component, not one segment.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton disabled secondaryActionLabel="More options" sections={alternatives} onClick={() => create()}>
  Create
</SplitButton>

examples.name: Forwarding other Button props
examples.description: Every other ButtonProps prop (tone, iconBefore, iconAfter, any native button attribute) forwards straight to the primary action via {...rest}.
examples.jsx:
<SplitButton
  tone="warning"
  iconBefore={<AlertIcon decorative />}
  secondaryActionLabel="More options"
  sections={alternatives}
  onClick={() => flagForReview()}
>
  Flag for review
</SplitButton>

antiExamples.name: Using Split Button for a single action with no alternatives
antiExamples.reason: sections is meant for a small group of closely related alternatives, not an empty placeholder - a single action with no alternatives should use Button directly instead of carrying an unused caret segment.

antiExamples.name: Expecting an auto-derived secondary action label
antiExamples.reason: secondaryActionLabel is required, not derived from children - the caret segment has no visible text of its own to derive an accessible name from. TypeScript rejects this at compile time.

antiExamples.name: Expecting a 'subtle' appearance
antiExamples.jsx:
<SplitButton appearance="subtle" secondaryActionLabel="More options" sections={alternatives} onClick={() => create()}>
  Create
</SplitButton>
antiExamples.reason: appearance is deliberately narrower than Button's own ('default' | 'primary' only) - Figma never shows a subtle split button, so code doesn't invent one. TypeScript rejects this at compile time.

examples.name: Unbounded list, no overflow
examples.description: maxVisible omitted - every tag renders, wrapping onto new lines as the row fills.
examples.jsx:
<TagGroup
  tags={[
    { id: 'trust', label: 'Averill Family Living Trust', tone: 'green', href: '/trusts/1' },
    { id: 'asset', label: "Ben's Investments", tone: 'blue', href: '/assets/1' },
    { id: 'task', label: 'Follow-up task', tone: 'teal', href: '/tasks/12' },
  ]}
/>

examples.name: Truncated list with a '+N more' overflow tag
examples.description: The common case - once tags.length exceeds maxVisible, the rest collapse behind an overflow tag that opens a Dropdown Menu.

examples.name: Overflow tag leading instead of trailing
examples.description: alignment='right' matches Figma's alignment=right variant - the overflow tag renders before the visible tags, same tags visible either way.

examples.name: Acting on a selected truncated tag
examples.description: Tag Group never assumes what selection means - wire onOverflowTagSelect to navigate, remove, or anything else.

examples.name: Removable tags in a bounded group
examples.description: Each TagGroupItem's own isRemovable/onRemove forwards straight to the rendered Tag, unaffected by truncation.
examples.jsx:
<TagGroup
  tags={[
    { id: 'vacation-home', label: 'Vacation Home', isRemovable: true, onRemove: () => handleRemove('vacation-home') },
    { id: 'rental', label: 'Rental Property', isRemovable: true, onRemove: () => handleRemove('rental') },
  ]}
/>

antiExamples.name: Setting size on an individual tag item
antiExamples.reason: TagGroupItem omits size from Tag's own props - Tag Group applies one size uniformly via TagGroupProps.size, including to the overflow tag. There is no per-item size mixing, matching Figma's own tab-group example.

antiExamples.name: Expecting a truncated tag's selection to navigate automatically
antiExamples.reason: Selecting a truncated tag from the overflow panel only calls onOverflowTagSelect(tag, event) - Tag Group does not read the tag's own href and navigate for you, the same 'never assume' rule Menu's own onSelect follows.

examples.name: Clearable with a real IconButton action
examples.jsx:
<TextField
  aria-label="Filter"
  value={value}
  onChange={(e) => setValue(e.target.value)}
  iconAfter={
    value ? (
      <IconButton appearance="subtle" shape="square" size="xs" aria-label="Clear" onClick={() => setValue('')}>
        <CloseIcon />
      </IconButton>
    ) : null
  }
/>

examples.name: Invalid with an error message
examples.jsx: Enter a valid email address

examples.name: Small size, subtle appearance (square bottom corners)
examples.jsx: <TextField size="sm" appearance="subtle" placeholder="Placeholder" aria-label="Small subtle field" />

antiExamples.name: No accessible name
antiExamples.reason: Placeholder text is not an accessible label - pair with a native label[htmlFor] or add aria-label.

antiExamples.name: Multi-line content
antiExamples.reason: Text Field has no textarea mode - it's for a single line of text.

antiExamples.name: Fixed set of options
antiExamples.reason: Use Select when the value comes from a fixed set of options instead of free text.

antiExamples.name: Faking a clear button with a bare icon
antiExamples.reason: A bare icon with a click handler is not a real, focusable, labeled control. Use a real IconButton (appearance=subtle, shape=square) instead.

examples.name: Basic action menu from a button
examples.description: The common case - a button trigger opening a searchable action list.

examples.name: Icon-button row menu, no search
examples.description: A dense row-level '...' menu - showSearch is false since a 3-4 item list doesn't need filtering.

examples.name: Right-aligned menu from a trailing trigger
examples.description: alignment='right' keeps the panel from overflowing past the trigger's right edge when the trigger sits near the end of a row.
examples.jsx:
<DropdownMenu
  aria-label="Table row actions"
  open={open}
  onOpenChange={setOpen}
  alignment="right"
  showSearch={false}
  sections={[{ id: 'actions', items: rowActionItems }]}
>
  <IconButton aria-label="Row actions" onClick={() => setOpen((current) => !current)}>
    <MoreVertIcon size="sm" decorative />
  </IconButton>
</DropdownMenu>

antiExamples.name: Passing a content prop the way Popup allows
antiExamples.reason: DropdownMenu has no content prop - it always renders a Menu built from sections. For arbitrary non-Menu floating content, compose Popup directly instead of forcing it through DropdownMenu.

antiExamples.name: Expecting a selection to close the dropdown automatically
antiExamples.jsx:
<DropdownMenu open={open} onOpenChange={setOpen} sections={[{ id: 'a', items: [{ id: 'delete', label: 'Delete', onSelect: handleDelete }] }]}>
  <Button onClick={() => setOpen(true)}>Actions</Button>
</DropdownMenu>
antiExamples.reason: Neither Menu nor DropdownMenu calls onOpenChange on selection. Clicking 'Delete' here runs handleDelete but leaves the dropdown open - call setOpen(false) from inside onSelect instead.

examples.name: Basic action menu
examples.description: A plain list of action rows with leading icons, no search or selection.
examples.jsx:
<Menu
  aria-label="Matter actions"
  showSearch={false}
  sections={[
    {
      id: 'actions',
      items: [
        { id: 'rename', label: 'Rename', leadingElement: <EditIcon spacing="spacious" decorative />, onSelect: handleRename },
        { id: 'duplicate', label: 'Duplicate', leadingElement: <CopyIcon spacing="spacious" decorative />, onSelect: handleDuplicate },
        { id: 'delete', label: 'Delete', leadingElement: <DeleteIcon spacing="spacious" decorative />, onSelect: handleDelete },
      ],
    },
  ]}
/>

examples.name: Searchable menu with a heading
examples.description: The default searchable shape, filtering a named section by typed text.

examples.name: Checkbox-style multi-select section
examples.description: Each row independently opts into selectionType='checkbox'; the leading glyph is Figma's own CheckboxFillIcon/CheckboxEmptyIcon, colored selected/subtle to match - not a real Checkbox control.

examples.name: Radio-style single-select section
examples.description: Each row opts into selectionType='radio'; only the consumer's own state ensures a single selected row. The leading glyph is Figma's own RadioCheckedIcon/RadioUncheckedIcon.

examples.name: Selection closes a containing Dropdown Menu
examples.description: Menu never closes anything itself - wire onOpenChange(false) from each item's own onSelect.
examples.jsx:
<Menu
  aria-label="Matter actions"
  showSearch={false}
  sections={[{
    id: 'actions',
    items: [{
      id: 'delete',
      label: 'Delete',
      onSelect: () => {
        handleDelete();
        setOpen(false);
      },
    }],
  }]}
/>

examples.name: Loading state
examples.description: Replaces the sections area with a Spinner and a custom label while data loads.
examples.jsx: <Menu aria-label="Matter actions" loading loadingLabel="Loading matters…" showSearch={false} sections={[]} />

antiExamples.name: Nesting a real Checkbox inside leadingElement
antiExamples.jsx:
<Menu
  aria-label="View options"
  sections={[{
    id: 'view',
    items: [{
      id: 'showDrafts',
      label: 'Show drafts',
      selectionType: 'checkbox',
      selected: checked,
      leadingElement: <Checkbox checked={checked} onChange={handleToggle} />,
    }],
  }]}
/>
antiExamples.reason: Each row renders as a real <button>. Nesting Checkbox's real <input> inside it is invalid HTML (a focusable control inside another one) and creates two conflicting ways to activate the same row - one via the button's own onClick, one via the checkbox's onChange. Use a decorative icon/glyph instead and let selected/selectionType carry the real state, or toggle the row's own onSelect.

antiExamples.name: Expecting Menu to close a containing Dropdown Menu
antiExamples.jsx:
<DropdownMenu open={open} onOpenChange={setOpen}>
  <Button>Actions</Button>
  <Menu sections={[{ id: 'a', items: [{ id: 'delete', label: 'Delete', onSelect: handleDelete }] }]} />
</DropdownMenu>
antiExamples.reason: Menu has no idea it's inside a Dropdown Menu and never calls onOpenChange itself. Clicking 'Delete' here runs handleDelete but leaves the dropdown open - call setOpen(false) from inside onSelect instead.
